author: Joan Didion
zh_title: 《奇想之年》：事情已经发生，生活却还没有跟上
en_title: The Year of Magical Thinking: Life Has Not Caught Up with What Happened
zh_deck: 留下的鞋、反复回来的晚饭、仍想告诉丈夫的新事。事实已经确认，生活却要在许多地方重新承认它。
en_deck: Shoes kept for a return, an ordinary dinner, something still to tell him: knowing a fact and living with it move at different speeds.

zh_body:
丈夫去世以后，狄迪恩整理他的衣物，却没能把鞋送走。她忽然明白，自己还在为他回来作准备：人回来了，总得有鞋穿。这个念头经不起推敲，她也知道，但知道并没有立刻使它消失。

《奇想之年》最令人难忘的，大概就是这种同时存在的清醒与不清醒。作者并没有把死亡误认成一次远行。她处理了许多必须处理的事情，能够向别人说明发生了什么；可是，一旦碰到一双鞋，日常生活里仍有另一个她，不肯照着已经确认的事实往下走。

2003年12月30日，狄迪恩与丈夫约翰·格雷戈里·邓恩从医院回家。他们的女儿金塔纳病得很重，正在接受救治。夫妇二人坐下吃晚饭时，约翰突发心脏病，骤然离世。他们结婚将近四十年，都是作家，长期在家工作。失去的不只是每天会见面的亲人，还有那个几乎一直在旁边、随时可以接着说话的人。

书名里的“奇想”，指向她在这之后产生的种种不合道理的盼望。它并非对神秘力量的赞美，而是一位习惯查证、分析和写作的人，发现自己竟会相信某些连自己也无法辩护的念头。书写到的正是这一年的反复：头脑已经承认的事，身体、习惯与愿望还在一次次重新遇见。

## 她为什么反复回到那顿晚饭

狄迪恩在开篇一再留意，出事前的一切有多么寻常。晚饭并没有预先换上一副悲剧的面孔。也正因为如此，回忆很难把那一刻安置妥当：既然此前仍在过日子，怎么会忽然再也不能过下去？

通常我们讲一个已经结束的故事，会挑出征兆，把后来发生的事接到前面去。狄迪恩却不断碰见接不上的地方。她记得一些细节，对另一些又没有把握；越想准确重述，就越不能把它说成一段早已安排好起承转合的往事。读者也因此无法舒舒服服地站到结局外面，说一句“原来如此”。

她的记者习惯在这里没有失效，却也不再足够。追查事实可以减少误解，不能把事实改成另一种结果。我们读到的不是一个人不肯动脑，而是一个人反复使用最熟练的本领，希望在事情已经结束的地方，再找到一点能够做事的余地。

鞋子的念头由此显得更复杂了。它表面上像一个推理错误，背后却仍在维持家里原有的次序：这个人的东西应当在这里，因为这个人属于这里。把东西移走，仿佛就得亲手参与确认他的离开。对于旁观者，收拾是一项善后工作；对于当事人，它可能是一连串尚且承受不了的决定。

不过，狄迪恩没有要求读者把每一种迟疑都赞美为深情。她观察自己的念头，有时甚至近乎冷酷。这使文字没有被“因为太爱，所以如此”的解释盖住。爱当然在场，但她还要知道，自己究竟怎样逃开了已经知道的事。她写不出一个能使矛盾消失的答案，便把矛盾留在那里。

## 能把事情办好，不等于已经承受得住

约翰去世以后，女儿的病情仍在变化，狄迪恩不能只留在回忆中。看医生、理解病情、安排后续照料，现实一直在向她提出问题。书里因此并置着两种很不相称的声音：一边是精确的名称与事实，一边是无法使自己相信某件事的内心。

文学评论家 John Leonard 在当年的书评中，特别注意到医学用语、诗句和记忆碎片的交错。这个观察有助于理解本书的读法。那些名词不是作者忽然变得冷漠的证据；它们也是她在混乱里寻找可以抓住的东西。懂得一个词，至少暂时知道了别人正在谈什么，接下来或许还能问一个问题。

但她也写出了一种难堪：懂得怎样询问、怎样办理手续，容易让旁人以为，她应当能够应付眼前的灾难。熟练的动作遮住了里面的不知所措。于是，能力越是还能维持，一个人的困境有时反而越难被看见。

可是，女儿还需要她。她不能等到完全承受住丈夫的死亡，再去理解医生的话。两件事挤在同一段日子里，使“能够应付”的意思变得很有限：有些事办成了，生活却远没有因此安顿下来。

《奇想之年》对此的呈现，并不靠不断提高情绪的音量。一个细节回来一次，意义便发生一点变化。读者前面觉得她已经明白了，后面才发现，“明白”并没有一次完成。若期待一部由受创到康复、每一章都比上一章好些的回忆录，就可能对这种往返不耐烦。可是，把它整理得更顺，反而会损失她努力留下的经验。

书中也没有一份可供照做的哀伤程序。她面对女儿的病，面对丈夫的缺席，两件事纠缠着进行，各有不能代替的困难。把这种生活概括成“她需要时间”，不能算错，只是省去了时间里实际发生的事情。

## 没有人接着听的那句话

比起死亡发生的那一天，有些读者可能更能理解死亡之后一个很小的变化：遇到什么事，仍想告诉那个人，随即才想起，已经无法告诉他了。

狄迪恩在后来接受 Terry Gross 采访时谈过这一点。她也说，自己并不特别害怕独处。困难不在于房子终于安静下来，而在于生活仍然不断生出要与约翰分享的话。独处的能力和失去一个人的痛苦，原来并不互相抵消。

这个区别使我们重新看见书中的婚姻。如果只说他们感情深厚，仍然太笼统。两个人一起写作、一起变老，许多经历已经有了共同的背景，不必从头解释。旁人也许能倾听，却需要她先把人物、来龙去脉和旧日的自己重新交代一遍。那个原本不需要交代的世界，现在忽然多出了大量前言。

这种缺席还会随着新的日子不断出现。回忆可以保存他们已经说过的话，却不能替约翰回答此后发生的新事。她仍会有新的见闻，仍会想到他可能怎样回应；只是，从前可以再问他一句，如今只能由自己想下去。共同生活于是渐渐有了两种时间：一部分停在那里，另一部分不得不继续。

书里的婚姻也由此超出了“彼此陪伴”几个字。陪伴久了，会成为说话和思考的习惯。狄迪恩不是在替依赖作抽象辩护，她只是让我们看见，这些习惯曾经如何使两个人能够一起生活，又在只剩一个人时，怎样不断碰空。

当然，这只是狄迪恩这段婚姻的自述。她的家庭资源、文化生活与长年共同工作的条件，并不属于每一位丧偶者。有读者觉得这些具体背景使文字更真切，也有人因为其中的名人、场所与生活方式感到疏远。这样的阅读分歧值得保留。承认她的痛苦，不要求我们把她的生活当作所有人的样本；觉得自己没有被代表，也不必据此否认这份记录。

## 写成一本书以后

有一个时间上的区别，介绍本书时不能省略。金塔纳是在书稿完成之后、出版之前去世的。狄迪恩后来另写了《蓝夜》，同名舞台剧也有自己的处理。因此，不能把《奇想之年》当成她回顾所有这些丧失之后写出的总账。

她在采访中解释，没有因女儿的去世改写已经完成的书，因为这本书属于一段特定的时间，讲的是一段婚姻。这种坚持也为读者留下了一道界限：书可以结束，生活却不会因为作者已经找到了结尾，就停止发生新事。

同样需要分清的，是写作与康复的关系。在《巴黎评论》的访谈里，狄迪恩谈到这部书如何依靠反复修改形成回声。那些看似不断绕回原处的句子，有写作上的经营，并非把日记原封不动地交给出版社。她花力气使读者能够进入这段混乱，却没有因此获得对日后生活的保证。

这种经过经营的反复，也让读者有机会体会时间在书里怎样流逝。日期已经往后走，一句话却把叙述带回原来的晚上。前面看似多余的重述，到了这里才显出必要：她不是缺少一个事实，而是同一个事实，在生活的不同地方都要重新发生一遍。

读《奇想之年》，不一定要正在经历丧失。对于还在陪伴别人的人，它也能改变一些细小的判断。听见对方把同一件事说了一遍又一遍，我们未必还会急着提醒“你之前说过了”。重复有时不是忘记已经讲过，而是那件事到现在仍没有讲完。

至于那双留下的鞋，我们不必替狄迪恩规定一个应当清走它的日子。她已经把最难说明的部分写出来了：知道一个人不会再回来，与学会在他不会回来的生活里度日，中间还有许多个寻常的晚上。
en_body:
After her husband died, Joan Didion sorted through his clothes but could not give away his shoes. She realized that she was still preparing for his return: he would need shoes when he came back. The thought could not survive scrutiny. She knew that, but knowing did not make it disappear.

Perhaps the most memorable thing about The Year of Magical Thinking is this coexistence of lucidity and its opposite. Didion had not mistaken death for a journey. She dealt with practical necessities and could explain what had happened. Yet a pair of shoes brought forward another part of her, unable to proceed according to the established facts.

On December 30, 2003, Didion and her husband, John Gregory Dunne, returned from visiting their seriously ill daughter, Quintana, in hospital. As they sat down to dinner, John suffered a fatal heart attack. Married for nearly forty years, both writers, they had long worked at home. She lost not only a loved person she saw every day but someone almost always nearby, available for the next sentence.

First published in 2005, the book follows the unreasonable hopes that emerged afterward. Its title does not celebrate supernatural powers. It describes a writer accustomed to investigation and analysis discovering beliefs she could not defend even to herself. Throughout this year, body, habit, and desire repeatedly encounter something the mind has already acknowledged.

## Why she keeps returning to dinner

Early in the book, Didion repeatedly notices how ordinary everything was before the event. Dinner had not dressed itself as tragedy in advance. That ordinariness makes the moment difficult to settle in memory. If they were still living their lives, how could continuing those lives become impossible so suddenly?

When telling a story whose ending we know, we usually select signs that connect the outcome to what preceded it. Didion encounters connections that will not hold. Some details remain clear, others uncertain. Trying to recount events accurately prevents them from becoming a neatly prepared narrative with a beginning, middle, and end. The reader cannot stand comfortably outside it and announce an explanation.

Her journalistic habits still work, but they are no longer sufficient. Investigation can correct misunderstandings; it cannot produce a different outcome. She is not refusing to think. She keeps using her best-developed ability, hoping to discover some remaining possibility of action where events have already ended.

The shoes become more complicated in this light. What resembles an error of reasoning also sustains the household's familiar order: his things belong here because he belongs here. Removing them would make her participate in confirming his departure. For an observer, sorting possessions is an administrative task. For the person doing it, each decision may still be unbearable.

Didion nevertheless does not ask us to admire every hesitation as devotion. Her examination of her thoughts can be almost merciless. Love is present, but saying that she behaves this way because she loved deeply would obscure her question: how did she evade something she already knew? Unable to dissolve the contradiction, she leaves it visible.

## Managing things is not the same as bearing them

Quintana's condition continued to change after John's death. Didion could not remain entirely within memory. Doctors, medical explanations, and arrangements for care kept making demands. The book therefore places two incongruous voices together: precise names and facts beside an inner inability to believe what has occurred.

In his contemporary review, John Leonard noticed the interweaving of medical terminology, poetry, and fragments of memory. His observation helps explain how the book works. Technical terms are not evidence that Didion has become unfeeling. They give her something to hold in confusion. Understanding a word means, briefly, knowing what others are discussing and perhaps being able to ask another question.

Yet knowing how to ask and arrange things can lead others to assume that she can manage the catastrophe itself. Practiced actions conceal bewilderment. As long as someone's competence remains intact, their distress may become harder to see.

Her daughter still needs her. She cannot finish absorbing her husband's death before learning what the doctors mean. The demands occupy the same days. Under these conditions, coping means something very limited: certain things get done without life becoming settled.

The book conveys this without continually raising its emotional volume. A returning detail changes slightly in meaning. We thought she understood earlier; later we discover that understanding was not accomplished once and for all. Readers expecting an orderly movement from injury to recovery may find the repetition frustrating. Straightening it out, however, would erase the experience she is trying to preserve.

Nor does the book supply a procedure for grief. Her daughter's illness and her husband's absence proceed together, presenting different, irreplaceable difficulties. Saying that she needs time is not wrong. It simply leaves out what happens inside that time.

## The sentence with no one there to hear it

Some readers may recognize a small change after death more readily than the moment of death itself: something happens, you want to tell that person, and only then remember that you cannot.

In a later interview with Terry Gross, Didion discussed this experience. She also explained that being alone did not particularly frighten her. The difficulty was not finally having a quiet house. Life kept producing things she wanted to share with John. The ability to be alone did not cancel the pain of losing him.

This distinction reveals more about the marriage than a general statement of affection could. Writing and growing older together had given them a shared background. Other people might listen, but first she would need to introduce the characters, explain earlier events, and reconstruct who she had been. A world that once needed no introduction suddenly required extensive preliminaries.

New days keep generating new forms of absence. Memory preserves what they already said but cannot supply John's responses to later events. She still encounters things and imagines his reaction. Previously she could ask; now she must continue the conversation alone. Shared life acquires two times: one remains where it was, while the other has to move.

Companionship, sustained over years, becomes a habit of speech and thought. Didion is not making an abstract defense of dependence. She shows how such habits helped two people live together and how, with only one person remaining, they repeatedly reach toward someone who is not there.

This is still her account of a particular marriage. Its resources, cultural setting, and years of working together are not shared by every bereaved spouse. Some readers find these details convincing; others feel distanced by the celebrities, places, and way of life. Both responses have room here. Acknowledging her pain does not require treating her life as everyone's model, and feeling unrepresented need not invalidate the record.

## After the book is finished

One chronological distinction matters. Quintana died after the manuscript was completed but before publication. Didion later wrote Blue Nights; the stage adaptation of The Year of Magical Thinking also makes its own choices. The memoir is not a retrospective reckoning written after all these losses.

In an interview, Didion explained why she had not rewritten it following her daughter's death: it concerned a particular period and a marriage. Her decision preserves a boundary. A book can end without life agreeing to stop producing events because its author has found a conclusion.

Writing must also be distinguished from recovery. In The Paris Review, Didion described the revision that created the book's echoes. Sentences that seem to circle back have been deliberately composed; this is not an unedited diary. She worked to make confusion accessible without thereby securing any guarantee about her future.

That shaped repetition lets us experience how time passes in the book. Dates advance; a sentence returns us to the same evening. Restatements that seemed unnecessary become essential. She is not missing a fact. The same fact has to happen again in different parts of her life.

One need not be bereaved to read the book. It can alter small judgments made while accompanying someone else. Hearing a person tell the same thing again, we may hesitate before pointing out that they already told us. Repetition does not always mean forgetting a previous telling. Sometimes the event has still not finished being told.

As for the shoes, we need not assign a date when Didion should have cleared them away. She has described the difficult interval: between knowing that someone will not return and learning to live where they will not return, there are still many ordinary evenings.
